title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The Mill and the Marshes: Opening the Tulliver World

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through George Eliot's great novel of the Tulliver family — chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
We'll be asking what makes it brilliant, what makes it heartbreaking, and why it still feels so urgently alive.
Joining me today are three people whose company I can think of no better reason to spend time with a novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose criticism is grounded in the conviction that great fiction is finally about character — about moral imagination — and not about social programme.
He reads Eliot with the rigour and the tenderness she deserves, and he will not let us reduce her.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the world the novel inhabits — the real institutions, the actual law, the grinding material conditions — into startling focus.
When James explains what it meant to lose a mill in the eighteen-thirties, you understand why this story feels like a wound.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read The Mill on the Floss as a teenager and has never quite stopped reading it.
She brings the reader's eye — and the reader's ear — to every sentence, and she will make sure we notice what is actually on the page.
Today we're opening the Tulliver world — the mill, the river, the family, and above all Maggie.
Let's begin.
The Mill on the Floss is, among many other things, a novel about the cost of being exceptional in a world that cannot accommodate you.
And Eliot establishes that cost with extraordinary economy very early on — in small scenes, in brief flashes of a child's inner life.
There is a passage that I find almost unbearably precise about how love curdled by jealousy operates in a child — in Maggie's response to Lucy.
Eliot writes — and the comedy here is perfectly calibrated —
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse is doing remarkable work there.
It locates Lucy's prettiness in the register of the decorative and the helpless — something to be petted rather than befriended.
And then Eliot shows us Maggie contemplating slapping Lucy — not out of cruelty exactly, but to wound Tom through her.
It is a perfectly truthful account of how children — how people — experience love under threat.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is how Eliot refuses to let us judge Maggie while absolutely showing us what Maggie is capable of.
The narrator holds two things at once — moral clarity and absolute sympathy.
And the syntax does so much of that work.
"It had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her" — that little clause carries everything.
Maggie was Lucy's champion before Tom made Lucy a rival.
The injustice of that — felt at seven years old — is the same injustice that will shadow Maggie's entire life.
She is always already losing something she earned.
I'd add that this dynamic between Maggie and Tom isn't merely psychological — it is structural.
Tom is sent away to be educated; Maggie stays home.
And yet when Maggie visits Tom at Mr Stelling's, the novel shows us in precise, almost comic detail that she is the more intellectually alive of the two.
Eliot describes how Maggie's questions about the Roman Empire — questions Tom would never have thought to ask — actually expanded his understanding.

"He had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
"A dim understanding" — that is Eliot at her most surgically dry.
Tom receives an expensive classical education and arrives at a dim understanding.
Maggie, who is given nothing, illuminates the room.
Quite so — and there is a beautiful tenderness in that same passage that one must not allow the satire to eclipse.
When Maggie is fetched away by Luke, Tom misses her — genuinely, grievously.
Eliot writes that "he had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons better, since she had been there."
The novel will not let Tom be simply the oppressor.
He is limited — severely limited — but he is also capable of love, of needing Maggie.
And the novel's final word on the two of them — carved, as it were, in stone — is only four words long.
"In their death they were not divided."
Everything the novel has built — every separation, every act of cruelty and tenderness — flows into that epitaph.
I can never read that line without feeling the full weight of what has happened to Maggie before those four words are even possible.
Because what precedes it — the moment of waking on the water, the dream, the terrible reckoning with herself — is so devastating.
Eliot writes of Maggie's awakening that "she had brought sorrow into the lives of others — into the lives that were knit up with hers by trust and love."
"Knit up" — it's such a domestic, physical word for those bonds.
And then she sees clearly what renunciation actually costs — not the quiet ecstasy she'd imagined, but "that sad, patient, loving strength which holds the clue of life."
The word clue — from the Latin, from the thread that leads you out of the labyrinth — is doing so much work there.
Maggie is lost — she has let go of the thread — and she knows it.
What that waking scene reveals, historically, is the impossibility of Maggie's position — not merely psychologically but materially and socially.
She has transgressed — or is perceived to have transgressed — in a world that offered women almost no path to self-determination.
She calls herself "an outlawed soul, with no guide but the wayward choice of her own passion."
Outlawed is the precise word — in the older sense, someone outside the protection of the law.
Women in Eliot's England who departed from the sanctioned path found themselves outside every system of social support.
The flood at the end is symbolic, yes — but it is also Eliot's recognition that the social world had no place for Maggie to return to.
And perhaps that is where we begin to see why this novel endures — it gives us a world of extraordinary richness and then shows us exactly how that world crushes its most alive inhabitant.
We'll be turning next to the textures of that world — the Dodson aunts, the social comedy, the provincial life that forms the pressure Maggie pushes against.
Stay with us.

segments.title: A Girl's Mind in a Boy's World: Maggie's Hunger for Knowledge

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, a close reading of George Eliot's extraordinary novel about growing up, growing into yourself, and the world's refusal to let you.
Today we're asking what it means to have a mind that outstrips its circumstances — and what the novel shows us about the price of that.
With me are three readers who bring very different lenses to this book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is finally about individual moral character — goodness tested, self-deception exposed.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world into the room — what the institutions were, what poverty actually meant, how the law worked.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel since her teens and returns to it with unfailing attention to what makes a sentence stop you cold.
We begin in St Ogg's, where minds are shaped — and constrained — by the world they're born into.
The passage that strikes me first in this segment is the narrator's portrait of Tulliver himself — a man whose self-image is entirely constructed by the flattery of his neighbours.
George Eliot is ruthless about this particular form of self-deception — the way social consensus becomes the mirror in which a man sees himself as prosperous.
The narrator puts it with magnificent economy — listen to this:

"He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance."
Jokes. Not evidence. Not achievement. Jokes.
That is a novelist doing sociology at the level of the individual psyche — showing precisely how a man comes to believe what is not true about himself.
And what makes that psychologically devastating is the legal reality underneath it — a two-thousand-pound mortgage on a freehold that Tulliver has essentially forgotten exists.
Eliot understands perfectly how provincial credit worked in the early Victorian period.
A miller with freehold land would be seen as creditworthy, and neighbours would borrow from him precisely because he appeared solid.
But those loans are exactly what prevent him from paying down the debt — so reputation and ruin feed each other, invisibly.
And then there is Basset itself — the portrait of that parish is as precise a piece of rural economics as you'll find in Victorian fiction.
Poor soil, poor roads, a non-resident landlord, a non-resident vicar — every institution that should support the community has absented itself.
What I find extraordinary is the way Eliot's satire in that Basset passage never loses its humanity.
She mocks the intellectual limitations of Basset's inhabitants, yes — but then she immediately catches herself, and asks us to catch ourselves too.
The narrator says she has nothing to urge against the abstract proposition that minds might triumph over circumstances — she only knows, in point of fact, they didn't.
That is Eliot at her most honest — and most devastating.
And it sets up everything about Maggie — who is precisely the mind that cannot triumph, not because she lacks the capacity, but because the world around her is Basset.
Which brings us to the Maggie of childhood — and one of the most remarkable single sentences in the novel.
It concerns the incident in which Maggie pushes the perfectly dressed Lucy Deane into the mud.
In any other novelist's hands, this would be a comic set-piece or a moral cautionary moment.
Eliot does something astonishing — she embeds a full meditation on the nature of tragedy in a single sentence about a small girl:

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action."
The Greek phrase — τι μέγεθος — is Aristotle's term for the scale of action that tragedy requires.
Maggie has the passion of a tragic heroine; she simply lacks the stage.
That sentence makes me stop every single time I read it.
Because what Eliot is doing is honouring Maggie's inner life completely — taking it seriously as tragedy — while simultaneously showing us its comic, muddy, eight-year-old exterior.
Poor little pink-and-white Lucy in the cow-trodden mud — the detail is perfect.
Lucy is always presented through her surfaces — her appearance, her social conformity.
Maggie, by contrast, is all interior — all depth, all want — and that is precisely her problem in a world that rewards surfaces.
And the novel shows us systematically what that costs a girl who is all interior.
There is a passage later — when Maggie is older but still a child — where Eliot describes the texture of her daily suffering with what I can only call clinical precision.
Maggie has retreated upstairs in tears after another encounter with the world's indifference.
And the narrator observes — here Edmund has quoted the Aristotle, so let me offer this companion passage:
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
"Though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present."
That final clause is a rebuke directed at the reader — at us — for every time we have dismissed a young person's anguish as temporary.
That is the Eliot that commands my deepest admiration — the moralist who refuses to let comfortable readers feel comfortable.
What I find significant about that passage is the detail: in books there were people who were always agreeable or tender, and who did not show their kindness by finding fault.
Maggie has educated her expectations on fiction.
And the world has declined to meet them.
This is not sentimentality on Eliot's part — it is a precise diagnosis of what it means to be a reader in a world that does not read you back.
And then the novel jumps forward to show us what becomes of that hunger — that need for a world equal to her inner life.
The boat scene with Stephen Guest is one of the most physically beautiful passages Eliot ever wrote.
And I want to read just the heart of it, because the prose enacts the very thing it describes — a consciousness drifting, dissolving:
"The breath of the young, unwearied day, the delicious rhythmic dip of the oars, the fragmentary song of a passing bird heard now and then, as if it were only the overflowing of brimful gladness."
"The sweet solitude of a twofold consciousness that was mingled into one by that grave, untiring gaze which need not be averted."
A twofold consciousness mingled into one — that is what Maggie has been aching for her entire life.
To be seen. Wholly.
And the tragedy, of course, is that the world's wife is waiting on the bank — as the next chapter makes devastatingly clear.
The passage about St Ogg's receiving Maggie back after the boat trip is Eliot's most sustained piece of social satire in the novel.
She anatomises precisely how public opinion works — not by moral reasoning, but by outcome.
The narrator puts it simply and brutally:
"We judge others according to results; how else? — not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
Had Maggie returned as Mrs Stephen Guest, St Ogg's would have swallowed the whole episode with barely a murmur.
The moral content of the act is irrelevant. The social outcome is everything.
And public opinion in these cases, as the narrator dryly notes, is always of the feminine gender — not the world, but the world's wife.
It is a withering formulation — and entirely accurate, historically as well as morally.
But I want to end on Philip's letter — because it seems to me the only voice in the novel that fully meets Maggie where she is.
Philip writes to Maggie:
"You have been to my affections what light, what colour is to my eyes, what music is to the inward ear; you have raised a dim unrest into a vivid consciousness."
Raised a dim unrest into a vivid consciousness — that is what the novel itself does for us as readers.
And it is what Maggie has done, and been, for everyone in her orbit — often at catastrophic cost to herself.
Philip's letter undoes me every time.
Because he does what no one else in the novel manages — he sees her completely, and he releases her.
There is something stronger in you than your love for him — that is what he writes.
He is right about Maggie. The tragedy is that being right about her doesn't save her.
A dim unrest raised into a vivid consciousness — and a society that punishes it.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the novel's climax — the flood, the reunion, and what Eliot asks us to make of an ending that has divided readers from the day it was published.

segments.title: The Comedy of Provincial Life: Social Pretension and Domestic Friction

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're looking at something that doesn't always get its due — the comedy in this novel.
George Eliot is remembered for tragedy, for moral seriousness — but she is also wickedly, precisely funny.
With me today are three readers who know this novel deeply and will not let its pleasures go unexamined.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and defender of the novel as moral imagination rather than social programme.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who will keep us honest about what provincial life in this era actually looked like.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel since her teens, who attends above all to what makes you stop and read a sentence twice.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because I think you'd argue that the comedy here is inseparable from the characterisation.
Yes — and I'd start with Tom, which might surprise people who think of him as merely the difficult brother.
There's a passage early on where the narrator describes his entirely unremarkable, ordinary face — cream and roses, indeterminate nose — and then pulls a wonderful reversal.
The narrator says Nature has a deep cunning hiding itself under the appearance of openness.
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
Turn off by the gross — as if Nature were a factory producing identical lads.
That image is absolutely comic, and yet it does real work — it tells us everything about Tom's hidden stubbornness before we've seen much of it.
The joke is the argument.
That conflation of comedy and character analysis is where Eliot is at her most Shakespearean, I think.
Tom's face refuses to be formidable — and Eliot returns to that word formidable with a kind of gleeful persistence.

Later, when Tom dresses himself up as a fierce warrior with burnt cork eyebrows and a red turban, the narrator notes that his pink cheeks refused to look formidable, let him frown as he would before the looking-glass.
"Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead."
There is something deeply, tenderly funny about that boy at the looking-glass, willing his face into menace.
And yet — it is also a portrait of a will that will not accept the limits of what it has been given.
That is Tom Tulliver entire.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, if I may.
The comedy in this novel is almost always socially located — it comes with a postcode, if you like.
Take Bob Jakin's speech to Mrs Glegg — because that is a perfectly observed piece of commercial flattery.
Bob tells her it's a thousand pities she shouldn't deal with a packman instead of going into these newfangled shops.

"it's a thousand pities such a lady as you shouldn't deal with a packman, i' stead o' goin' into these newfangled shops, where there's half-a-dozen fine gents wi' their chins propped up wi' a stiff stock, a-looking like bottles wi' ornamental stoppers."
Bottles with ornamental stoppers — that is a phrase good enough to make a social historian actually laugh aloud.
Bob is describing the new retail trade of the 1820s and 30s — the rise of the draper's shop with its pretensions — and skewering it with absolute precision.
He is also, of course, comprehensively flattering Mrs Glegg at the same time — and she knows it, and doesn't quite mind.
And that's what makes Bob one of the great comic creations in the novel — he is utterly transparent and utterly effective simultaneously.
Mrs Glegg sees through him completely and he knows she does and charges ahead regardless.
But I keep coming back to Maggie, and to the passage about the hair-cutting, which I think is where Eliot's comedy gets genuinely philosophical.
After Maggie cuts her hair and is left weeping among her black locks, the narrator offers this astonishing defence of childhood suffering.

"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships; but it was not less bitter to Maggie—perhaps it was even more bitter—than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
Weather-worn mortals — that phrase alone is doing so much.
It's gently satirical about grown-up self-importance and entirely serious about the child's pain at the same moment.
That passage strikes me as one of the finest examples of what I'd call the narrator's double register in this novel.
She is simultaneously ironic and compassionate — not alternately, but at the same instant.
The comparison of Maggie to Ajax among the slaughtered sheep is, technically speaking, absurd — a small girl with a bad haircut set beside a Greek hero amid carnage.
And yet the heroic scale is precisely right — because the narrator has just persuaded us that the anguish is real, is proportionate, is not to be dismissed.
It is one of the most sophisticated comic effects in Victorian fiction.
There's a passage I'd add to this, which picks up on what Caroline said about Maggie and the outside world.
When Maggie runs away to find the gypsies, the comedy is built entirely from the gap between her self-conception and how she actually appears.
She gives away her only sixpence to a tramp, expecting him to feel very kindly toward her as a generous person.
He smiles and winks at his companion, and they both laugh loudly.
The narrator then observes — with perfect deadpan — that it was clear she was not likely to make a favourable impression on passengers.
"It was clear that she was not likely to make a favourable impression on passengers."
That understatement — after pages of Maggie's magnificent self-belief — is devastating in the most affectionate way.
And what I love is that she then worries about being mistaken for an idiot — which Tom had said her cropped hair made her look like.
So the comedy of the hair-cutting in the earlier passage is still reverberating — it has consequences that trail her into the next adventure.
Eliot is extraordinarily good at that — the way a comic episode leaves a deposit that makes the next scene funnier and sadder simultaneously.
That word — simultaneously — seems to be the one we keep arriving at.
Funny and sad, ironic and tender, comic and philosophical all at once.
We'll carry that thought forward as we turn now to the social architecture of St Ogg's — the aunts, the uncles, and the elaborate ritual of provincial respectability.

segments.title: The Ruin of the House: Commercial Failure and Family Collapse

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the great dramatic engines of the novel — the slow, grinding ruin of the Tulliver family.
Pride, law, money, and a miller's catastrophically poor judgment — all bearing down at once.
With me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral histories — stories of character tested, and sometimes broken, by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real institutional world into the conversation — what the law actually was, what debt actually meant.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it with the intimacy of long friendship.
Let's begin with Mr Tulliver's extraordinary letter to Mrs Glegg — perhaps the single act that most perfectly crystallises his self-destructive pride.
What strikes me first about that letter is its structural irony — and Eliot is exquisitely precise about the timing.
Mrs Glegg has just been basking in what the narrator calls her own lofty magnanimity — she has been generous, in her imagination at least.
And then the letter arrives that very evening — not the next week, not after reflection, but that very evening.
The narrator gives us the full substance of it, and I find it almost Johnsonian in its blunt courtesy.
Tulliver writes that she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come,
but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
He has offered the open door with one hand and slammed every other door shut with the other.
It is the gesture of a man who would rather be ruined on his own terms than saved on another's.
And what makes it comic as well as painful is that first sentence — the way Eliot implicates us directly.
She writes: Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I leave you to judge what effect was produced on her.
That is such a sly move.
We already know Mrs Glegg's pride intimately enough to supply the explosion ourselves.
And yet the sympathy is not entirely with Tulliver, is it.
He is doing real damage to his family's future with every stroke of that pen.
The five hundred pounds matters enormously here — that is not a symbolic sum.
For a working miller in the 1820s or 1830s, that is several years of income — a significant portion of his operating capital.
And he is promising to repay it within the month — before any lawsuit has concluded, before any security is assured.
This is how financial catastrophes propagate — not through single catastrophic decisions, but through a series of prideful gestures each entirely rational to the man making them.
And Eliot is careful to show us the precise mechanism by which Mrs Tulliver's pleading feeds into this ruinous trajectory.
The narrator offers us one of those perfectly pitched analogies — comparing her influence to a feather.
It might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back.
But the narrator will not allow us to rest with the easy reading — the blame lies not with the final feather but with all the previous weight.
It is a marvellous piece of philosophical precision wrapped in domestic comedy.
What I love about that passage is that Eliot is simultaneously defending and gently mocking Mrs Tulliver.
She is not powerful in herself — that phrase lands with a kind of sad honesty.
Her influence is entirely mediated through her husband's obsession with the Dodsons.
Whenever she departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of the Dodson family.
So she cannot even speak as herself — she is always ventriloquising the enemy in his mind.
There is something genuinely tragic about that, underneath the comedy.
And running through all of this is the figure of Wakem — who becomes, in Tulliver's mind, almost a supernatural malevolence.
The narrator gives us Tulliver's paranoid accounting — Wakem behind Pivart's irrigation, Wakem behind the road dispute, Wakem behind everything.
And then this wonderful, almost Dickensian portrait of the man himself — listen to how Eliot captures the texture of Tulliver's hatred.
A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!
That is free indirect discourse at its sharpest — we are inside Tulliver's fury and we can hear every syllable of his contempt.
And what makes it historically interesting is that Wakem is not simply a villain — he is a successful professional operating within entirely legal norms.
The law did not protect small millers from clever lawyers — it never had.
That connects directly to the portrait of Stelling — another man confidently ascending the professional ladder on borrowed substance.
Eliot's dissection of him is wickedly precise.
His doctrine had a tinge of evangelicalism, for that was the telling thing just then in the diocese.
Conviction is purely tactical — adjusted to market conditions.
Burke would have recognised the type immediately — the man who mistakes energy for character and ambition for vocation.
The economic logic of Stelling is beautifully rendered, and also historically exact.
Eliot sets it out with mock-syllogistic rigour — the furniture must be procured by some other means, or else the Reverend must go without them.
And then she offers the sentence that carries the whole chapter's satirical weight.
A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting.
Naturally — that word is doing extraordinary work.
Stelling's debt is presented as a logical consequence of ambition — almost as a mark of seriousness.
This is how the professional classes of the period actually thought — and it was Tulliver's children who paid the fees for that furniture and that wine.
And the cost of all these failures — Tulliver's lawsuit, Stelling's pretension — eventually comes to rest on Maggie.
There is a passage later in the novel that I keep returning to — after Tom's brutal treatment of her friendship with Philip.
Maggie retreats to her room, and the narrator traces the exact shape of her moral anguish.
She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict.
And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions.
The rhythm of that is devastating — the rise and the fall given equal weight.
And then her body gives her away — she beats the floor with her foot and tightens her fingers on her palm.
Eliot understands that grief of this kind is not quiet — it has to go somewhere.
And the narrator — later, reflecting on all of this — makes the moral argument explicit in one of the most powerful passages in the book.
It is a direct attack on the kind of rigid rule-following that has governed every character who has harmed Maggie — Tom above all.
Eliot writes — and this is worth sitting with —

the mysterious complexity of our life is not to be embraced by maxims, and that to lace ourselves up in formulas of that sort is to repress all the divine promptings and inspirations that spring from growing insight and sympathy.
That word lace is extraordinary — it implies constraint, even suffocation.
The man of maxims — Tom, the Dodsons, Stelling in his way — is not merely mistaken; he is actively suppressing what makes moral life possible.
I want to resist a wholly polemical reading of that passage — though I grant its power.
Eliot is not condemning principle as such — she is condemning principle unaccompanied by what she calls a hardly earned estimate of temptation.
Tom is not wrong to value duty — he is wrong to mistake the form of duty for its substance.
And that is a failure of imagination — which is precisely what Eliot the novelist is here to correct.
What I find remarkable is how the commercial and moral failures interlock — Tulliver's ruin is not just financial, it is a failure of exactly that imagination Edmund describes.
He cannot imagine how he looks to others — cannot imagine the world from inside Wakem's competence or Mrs Glegg's wounded pride.
And it is Maggie who inherits that deficit — who spends the whole novel trying to expand beyond what the world has made her.
We'll continue exploring that inheritance — and what it costs her — in the next section.

segments.title: Sibling Estrangement: The Widening Gulf Between Tom and Maggie

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the programme that takes George Eliot's great novel of provincial life and turns it over in the light.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most painful threads: the slow, almost inevitable estrangement of Tom and Maggie Tulliver.
To help us think through it, I'm joined by three exceptional readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads fiction as moral drama — who believes that character tested by circumstance is the real subject of any great novel.
Professor James Blackstone brings the social historian's eye — the law, the institutions, the real-world weight behind what Eliot depicts.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it with an intimacy that is, frankly, enviable.
Let's begin at the very opening of the book — where the narrator herself is already dreaming of a world she has lost.
What strikes me first, and what one never quite recovers from, is the way Eliot opens this novel — not with action, but with a confession of reverie.
The narrator wakes, as it were, from a dream and admits, with disarming candour, what has happened to her.
She tells us, in that famous opening passage:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The whole novel is announced in that gesture — the dreamer who cannot stay in the past, who must return to the present, benumbed from the effort of trying.
Every estrangement that follows — Tom's from Maggie, the family's from prosperity, the world's from innocence — is already implicit in that waking.
And what I love about that opening is how physical it is.
Benumbed arms. Elbows pressed into a chair. The body has paid the price of remembering.
Eliot doesn't give us nostalgia as a soft emotion — she gives it a cramp.
And that seems to me exactly right for a novel about Tom and Maggie, because their love for each other is never comfortable.
It is an ache. It always costs something.
I want to come at this from a different angle, if I may, because I think the estrangement between Tom and Maggie is inseparable from what happens to their father.
Tulliver's ruin is not merely financial. It is the ruin of a man's entire conception of himself and his place in the world.
And when that conception collapses, what Tom inherits is not property but grievance — and a father's demand for loyalty organised around that grievance.
There is a moment of terrible tenderness — Tulliver asking his wife simply for a kiss, for peace between them — and then he says something that cuts to the bone.
"We shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
The world has defeated him. And into that defeat, Tom steps — not as a son, exactly, but as an avenger.
James is right that the transfer of grievance is the key mechanism here. But I would press further into the moral texture of what Tulliver actually demands of Tom.
He does not merely ask for sympathy. He asks for something rather darker — a sworn inheritance of hatred.
He says of Wakem — and I think this is one of the most damning social portraits in the book:
"He's one o' them fine gentlemen as get money by doing business for poorer folks, and when he's made beggars of 'em he'll give 'em charity."
Now, Tulliver is not wrong about the mechanism. Eliot is too honest a writer to make his anger merely foolish.
But the demand that Tom write this hatred into the family Bible — that is where righteous anger tips into something that will poison the next generation.
Tom is an obedient son. And obedience, in this case, is a kind of moral catastrophe.
That phrase — 'write it i' the Bible' — I find it almost unbearable to read.
Because Tom does it. He carries it. And Maggie cannot.
That is the fault line between them — not temperament alone, but the fact that Tom has accepted a covenant that Maggie refuses.
And so when she comes to him and says — quite directly, quite bravely:
"I want you to absolve me from my promise about Philip Wakem. Or rather, I promised you not to see him without telling you. I am come to tell you that I wish to see him."
The courage of that. She has honoured the letter of her promise precisely in order to assert her right to break its spirit.
To Tom, this is betrayal. To Maggie, it is integrity. And both of them are right, which is what makes it so devastating.
Caroline puts her finger on something important about the moral logic here, but I'd want to name the social structure that underpins it.
Eliot gives us, in the Dodson and Tulliver world, a code of life that has remarkable internal coherence — and remarkable blindness.
She describes it with that wonderful satirical precision — their religion was, she says:

"of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it — if heresy properly means choice — for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
Like asthma. That is a devastating comparison — hereditary, wheezing, and fundamentally unexamined.
Tom has absorbed this code completely — duty, respectability, the claims of kin, the horror of social disgrace.
Maggie has absorbed it too — but she has also read beyond it, thought beyond it, and that is her crime in Tom's eyes.
I think James is correct, but I would add one defence of Tom — partial, and perhaps unfashionable.
The Dodson religion, as Eliot renders it, is not merely hypocrisy dressed up as virtue.
She is careful to say that it had its core of soundness — that honour was identified with integrity, thoroughness, faithfulness to admitted rules.
Tom is rigid, yes. He is unimaginative, certainly. But he is not contemptible — and Eliot never allows us to make him so.
The tragedy is not that Tom is a villain. The tragedy is that he is exactly what his world required him to be — and that world has no place for Maggie.
That is a distinction worth holding onto — not villainy, but a world that is simply too small for one of the people it has made.

We've moved from the narrator's dreaming wrist to a father's dying curse to a daughter's small, precise act of defiance — and the thread connecting all of it is a family that cannot contain what Maggie is.
We'll continue in a moment, looking at where that failure of containment finally breaks open.

segments.title: Words, Silence, and Unspoken Feeling: How Eliot Renders Emotional Truth

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
In this segment, we're looking at something Eliot does with extraordinary subtlety: how she renders emotional truth — not through grand declaration, but through the texture of a child's inner life.
We have four extraordinary chapters to draw on — all centred on Maggie and Tom as children, caught between imagination, pride, humiliation, and love.
With me, as always, is Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, who reads Eliot as a moralist of the first order.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who keeps us honest about what these children's lives actually meant in their world.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who hears every sentence as music.
Let's begin with Maggie's great escape — her resolution to run away to the gypsies.
What I love — and have loved since I first read this as a girl — is how Eliot captures the absolute logic of a child's misery.
The resolution doesn't begin as something small and sulky.
It begins — and the narrator is quite precise about this — on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
And then Eliot gives us the full glory of it.
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That "No!" at the start — it's almost audible as a child stamping her foot.
And yet it's not sentimental — Eliot is simultaneously inside Maggie's feeling and gently, precisely laughing at it.
Yes — and what is remarkable is that the comedy and the tragedy are entirely inseparable.
The narrator tells us that this was by no means a new idea to Maggie — that she had long contemplated gypsydom as her refuge.
She has been told she is "half wild" — and she has, with characteristic Maggie logic, taken that reproach and made it into a vocation.
The moral imagination at work here is Eliot's finest gift: she shows us that Maggie's fantasy is not mere childishness.
It is a genuine — if doomed — attempt at self-determination in a world that offers her no legitimate form of it.
And then there is the extraordinary detail of the letter she plans to send her father by a small gypsy messenger.
Even in her grand rebellion, she cannot abandon him.
There's something worth pausing on in that phrase — "escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances."
The gypsies, in the mid-nineteenth century, were the absolute boundary figure of English society — outside property, outside parish, outside respectability.
For Maggie to dream of joining them is not simply whimsy — it is a precise inversion of everything the Tullivers stand for.
And note that Tom has already dismissed the scheme with a very Tulliver practicality: gypsies were thieves, had nothing to eat, and only a donkey to drive.
Tom is already the voice of property and social calculation, even at nine years old.
And then the fantasy collapses — and the collapse is, I think, one of Eliot's funniest and most terrifying passages.
Maggie has been sitting with the gypsies for a matter of minutes before her view of them undergoes — as Eliot puts it — a rapid modification.
"She had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — I defy anyone to read those two words without a shudder and a laugh arriving at the same moment.
And then the suspicion that the fierce-eyed old man is, in fact, the Devil — who might turn into a fiery-eyed monster with dragon's wings.
Eliot never condescends to Maggie's terror — she takes it entirely seriously, even while rendering it comic.
The theological dimension there is genuinely remarkable.
Eliot tells us that Maggie wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded, whether — if the Devil were really present — he would know her thoughts.
"she wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded, whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts."
This is Eliot's wit at its most precise — a child in genuine mortal terror, and yet still thinking like a philosopher.
The instinct for inquiry cannot be suppressed even by fear.
This is what Caroline means by taking the child's inner life seriously — Eliot grants Maggie the dignity of a mind that works, however wildly it works.
The passage about Maggie's education is worth lingering on here — because Eliot is doing something quite sharp about how knowledge is distributed.
She sets up the contrast with devastating precision.
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
She knows what "polygamy" means, and has deduced the meaning of "poly" from first principles — but had no idea that gypsies were not well supplied with groceries.
That juxtaposition is not simply charming — it is a precise social observation about what a girl like Maggie could and could not access.
She had been to school for one year, and had so few books she sometimes read the dictionary.
That line is both funny and quietly devastating about the narrowness of opportunity for girls of her class.
"Her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams" — that sentence feels like a key to the whole novel.
Eliot is not being condescending — she is diagnosing with absolute precision what it means to be brilliant and unformed and female in that world.
And that diagnosis never leaves us for the rest of the book.
Let's turn now to Tom — because his humiliation at Mr Stelling's is rendered with a tenderness I find almost unbearable.
This passage contains, I think, one of the most quietly devastating sentences Eliot ever wrote about childhood.
Tom — proud, practical, physical Tom — has been broken down by the Latin supines for the fifth time.
And his sole resource — his last resort — is prayer.
But even prayer is hedged with the anxiety of propriety.
He rather shrank from the novelty and irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic for which he was not aware of any precedent.
Tom needs a precedent before he can pray for Latin.
That is characterisation of a very high order.
And when he finally does pray — the words are everything.
He has prayed for Maggie since she was a baby — and I find that unbearably moving.
And then the extempore addition, in the same low whisper —
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
"Please to make me." He is speaking to God like a child speaking to a parent who might just — if asked nicely enough — relent.
The cadence of that petition is heartbreaking in its humility.
What strikes me is the institutional critique embedded in the comedy.
Mr Stelling has lectured Tom very seriously about seizing the present golden opportunity of learning supines — otherwise he will regret it when he becomes a man.
The entire machinery of classical education — its premises, its punishments, its promises — is absurd when applied to a boy like Tom.
The education is not designed for him — it is designed to mark social distinction, not to cultivate understanding.
And Tom — clear-sighted enough to know that Stelling's standard is higher in the eyes of the world — is ground down by a system that was never built for his mind.
I would not entirely disagree with that — but I would add that Eliot is also doing something more delicate.
She writes that Tom became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before.
"strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before."
Eliot is not simply satirising an institution — she is watching what suffering does to the rigid categories of gender.
Tom in distress develops something of the girl's susceptibility — by which she means: a capacity to feel his own inadequacy acutely.
The humanity predominates, Eliot says — and in that small phrase she has the whole novel.
Beautifully said — and that phrase, "the human sensibilities predominated," feels like a touchstone for everything we've been discussing today.
Eliot's emotional truth is never simple — it holds comedy and tragedy, satire and tenderness, in the same sentence.
Thank you to Sir Edmund, Professor Blackstone, and Caroline for this conversation.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the world outside the family — to St Ogg's, and to what the town makes of the Tullivers.

segments.title: Duty, Desire, and Drowning: The Mill on the Floss in Retrospect

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing Maggie Tulliver's journey from that passionate, dark-haired child at the mill to the woman who chooses renunciation over happiness.
And I want to use this closing segment to ask the question the novel itself keeps circling: does George Eliot believe in what Maggie believes?
Edmund, you've been patient all episode with our various provocations. I'd like to start with you — and with Tom.
Thank you. And yes — Tom is where I want to begin, because I think the novel's moral architecture cannot be understood without him.

There is a passage early in the book — the moment when the family's ruin has just become clear to the children — that has always struck me as one of the most quietly devastating things Eliot ever wrote.
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank, — as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
Tom cannot weep. He holds his sister, but the grief is trapped inside him — rigid, unyielding.
And that image — the black curtain falling on his path — is not merely gothic atmosphere. It is a prophecy of character.
Tom's tragedy is that he never learns to weep. His virtue — his iron sense of duty — is also his limitation.
That image really does haunt the whole book, doesn't it? The curtain falls on Tom almost at the beginning, and it never quite lifts.
And yet — and I think this is what makes Eliot so uncomfortable to read — she doesn't let us simply condemn him.
There's that extraordinary scene where Aunt Glegg is at her most withering about Mr Tulliver, and Maggie is about to fly at her.
"Be quiet, Maggie," he said authoritatively, pushing her aside.
Two words. And they land like a verdict on the whole relationship.
But then Eliot tells us this is a 'remarkable manifestation of self-command and practical judgment in a lad of fifteen.' She means it sincerely.
Eliot holds both truths at once — Tom's authoritarianism and Tom's courage — and refuses to let us settle into simple feeling.
That refusal to settle is, I think, precisely what makes this a great novel rather than a tract.
Tom's 'practical judgment' is not incidental — it is what saves the family, materially speaking. The mill is reclaimed. The debt is paid.
Eliot understood exactly what economic competence meant in a world where ruin was permanent and disgrace was hereditary.
The tragedy is not that Tom is wrong about the world. The tragedy is that he is right about the world, and the world is wrong.
Yes — and that double irony extends to Maggie herself, doesn't it.
There is a moment — almost unbearably brief — when Mr Tulliver speaks to Maggie near the end of his life, and the weight of the whole novel seems to concentrate in a single line.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Seven words in dialect. And they close a door on everything he might have been, everything Maggie hoped for him.
No second chances. No redemption. Only the irreversibility of a life lived as it was lived.
That line destroys me every time. Because Maggie has been holding onto the hope of her father's restoration — spiritual, emotional, almost magical restoration.
And he simply — and gently — tells her: no. That is not how lives work.
It prepares us for everything Maggie does afterwards. Because Maggie, unlike her father, does try to live as though second chances are possible — for herself and for others.
And then comes the Stephen Guest catastrophe, and she has to reckon with what she has actually done.
And that reckoning is where the novel becomes most difficult — and, I would argue, most honest.
Maggie's speech to Stephen is not the language of a woman broken by society's judgment. It is her own moral code, applied to herself with extraordinary severity.
She says — and I want the words on the table, because they are so precisely argued —
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
This is not submission. This is a woman constructing an ethical position under enormous duress, and holding to it.
Whether Eliot endorses it entirely is another question. But she presents it with full force.
I find myself agreeing with James more than I expected to, and I want to say why.
There is a tendency among some readers — sympathetic readers — to treat Maggie's renunciation as a kind of defeat. As though Eliot is endorsing her society's cruelty.
But that speech to Stephen is not the voice of defeat. It is the voice of someone who has looked at what she has done to Lucy — to Philip — and cannot look away.
She says: 'I feel no excuse for myself, none.' That is not society speaking. That is conscience.
Eliot believes — as Johnson believed, as Burke believed — that the moral life is lived in the particular, in the face of the specific person you have wronged.
Yes — and there's that extraordinary cry at the end of the speech: 'Think of her ——'
"Oh, what is Lucy feeling now? She believed in me — she loved me — she was so good to me."
The argument breaks apart into pure feeling. The dash at the end — 'Think of her ——' — that unfinished sentence is Maggie overwhelmed by what she has done.
Eliot never lets the ethical argument become cold. The person is always there, at the end of the thought.
And that, perhaps, is where the novel's greatness lies — not in its answers but in its refusal to let the argument outlast the face.
Maggie Tulliver, Tom and his black curtain of cloud, Mr Tulliver who shall never live twice o'er — they stay with us because Eliot insists they are real people, not positions.
Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you. This has been a conversation I won't forget quickly.
For listeners: the novel is there to be reread. It rewards every return.
This has been The Mill on the Floss Unpacked. Thank you for listening.

c53:p1.text:
She had fallen asleep before nine, and had been sleeping for six hours before
the faintest hint of a midsummer daybreak was discernible. She awoke from that
vivid dreaming which makes the margin of our deeper rest. She was in a boat on
the wide water with Stephen, and in the gathering darkness something like a
star appeared, that grew and grew till they saw it was the Virgin seated in St
Ogg’s boat, and it came nearer and nearer, till they saw the Virgin was
Lucy and the boatman was Philip,—no, not Philip, but her brother, who
rowed past without looking at her; and she rose to stretch out her arms and
call to him, and their own boat turned over with the movement, and they began
to sink, till with one spasm of dread she seemed to awake, and find she was a
child again in the parlour at evening twilight, and Tom was not really angry.
From the soothed sense of that false waking she passed to the real
waking,—to the plash of water against the vessel, and the sound of a
footstep on the deck, and the awful starlit sky. There was a moment of utter
bewilderment before her mind could get disentangled from the confused web of
dreams; but soon the whole terrible truth urged itself upon her. Stephen was
not by her now; she was alone with her own memory and her own dread. The
irrevocable wrong that must blot her life had been committed; she had brought
sorrow into the lives of others,—into the lives that were knit up with
hers by trust and love. The feeling of a few short weeks had hurried her into
the sins her nature had most recoiled from,—breach of faith and cruel
selfishness; she had rent the ties that had given meaning to duty, and had made
herself an outlawed soul, with no guide but the wayward choice of her own
passion. And where would that lead her? Where had it led her now? She had said
she would rather die than fall into that temptation. She felt it now,—now
that the consequences of such a fall had come before the outward act was
completed. There was at least this fruit from all her years of striving after
the highest and best,—that her soul though betrayed, beguiled, ensnared,
could never deliberately consent to a choice of the lower. And a choice of
what? O God! not a choice of joy, but of conscious cruelty and hardness; for
could she ever cease to see before her Lucy and Philip, with their murdered
trust and hopes? Her life with Stephen could have no sacredness; she must
forever sink and wander vaguely, driven by uncertain impulse; for she had let
go the clue of life,—that clue which once in the far-off years her young
need had clutched so strongly. She had renounced all delights then, before she
knew them, before they had come within her reach. Philip had been right when he
told her that she knew nothing of renunciation; she had thought it was quiet
ecstasy; she saw it face to face now,—that sad, patient, loving strength
which holds the clue of life,—and saw that the thorns were forever
pressing on its brow. The yesterday, which could never be revoked,—if she
could have changed it now for any length of inward silent endurance, she would
have bowed beneath that cross with a sense of rest.
c53:p1.summary: Maggie awakens from a disturbing dream featuring Tom, Lucy, and Philip, and realizes the terrible consequences of her elopement with Stephen; she confronts her betrayal and begins her internal crisis of conscience.
c53:p1.best_quote: she had brought sorrow into the lives of others,—into the lives that were knit up with hers by trust and love

c8:p6.text:
For Mr Tulliver was in a position neither new nor striking, but, like other
everyday things, sure to have a cumulative effect that will be felt in the
long run: he was held to be a much more substantial man than he really was. And
as we are all apt to believe what the world believes about us, it was his habit
to think of failure and ruin with the same sort of remote pity with which a
spare, long-necked man hears that his plethoric short-necked neighbour is
stricken with apoplexy. He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about
his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of
land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of
considerable substance. They gave a pleasant flavour to his glass on a
market-day, and if it had not been for the recurrence of half-yearly payments,
Mr Tulliver would really have forgotten that there was a mortgage of two
thousand pounds on his very desirable freehold. That was not altogether his own
fault, since one of the thousand pounds was his sister’s fortune, which
he had to pay on her marriage; and a man who has neighbours that  will  go
to law with him is not likely to pay off his mortgages, especially if he enjoys
the good opinion of acquaintances who want to borrow a hundred pounds on
security too lofty to be represented by parchment. Our friend Mr Tulliver had
a good-natured fibre in him, and did not like to give harsh refusals even to
his sister, who had not only come in to the world in that superfluous way
characteristic of sisters, creating a necessity for mortgages, but had quite
thrown herself away in marriage, and had crowned her mistakes by having an
eighth baby. On this point Mr Tulliver was conscious of being a little weak;
but he apologised to himself by saying that poor Gritty had been a good-looking
wench before she married Moss; he would sometimes say this even with a slight
tremulousness in his voice. But this morning he was in a mood more becoming a
man of business, and in the course of his ride along the Basset lanes, with
their deep ruts,—lying so far away from a market-town that the labour of
drawing produce and manure was enough to take away the best part of the profits
on such poor land as that parish was made of,—he got up a due amount of
irritation against Moss as a man without capital, who, if murrain and blight
were abroad, was sure to have his share of them, and who, the more you tried to
help him out of the mud, would sink the further in. It would do him good rather
than harm, now, if he were obliged to raise this three hundred pounds; it would
make him look about him better, and not act so foolishly about his wool this
year as he did the last; in fact, Mr Tulliver had been too easy with his
brother-in-law, and because he had let the interest run on for two years, Moss
was likely enough to think that he should never be troubled about the
principal. But Mr Tulliver was determined not to encourage such shuffling
people any longer; and a ride along the Basset lanes was not likely to enervate
a man’s resolution by softening his temper. The deep-trodden hoof-marks,
made in the muddiest days of winter, gave him a shake now and then which
suggested a rash but stimulating snarl at the father of lawyers, who, whether
by means of his hoof or otherwise, had doubtless something to do with this
state of the roads; and the abundance of foul land and neglected fences that
met his eye, though they made no part of his brother Moss’s farm,
strongly contributed to his dissatisfaction with that unlucky agriculturist. If
this wasn’t Moss’s fallow, it might have been; Basset was all
alike; it was a beggarly parish, in Mr Tulliver’s opinion, and his
opinion was certainly not groundless. Basset had a poor soil, poor roads, a
poor non-resident landlord, a poor non-resident vicar, and rather less than
half a curate, also poor. If any one strongly impressed with the power of the
human mind to triumph over circumstances will contend that the parishioners of
Basset might nevertheless have been a very superior class of people, I have
nothing to urge against that abstract proposition; I only know that, in point
of fact, the Basset mind was in strict keeping with its circumstances. The
muddy lanes, green or clayey, that seemed to the unaccustomed eye to lead
nowhere but into each other, did really lead, with patience, to a distant
high-road; but there were many feet in Basset which they led more frequently to
a centre of dissipation, spoken of formerly as the “Markis o’
Granby,” but among intimates as “Dickison’s.” A large
low room with a sanded floor; a cold scent of tobacco, modified by undetected
beer-dregs; Mr Dickison leaning against the door-post with a melancholy
pimpled face, looking as irrelevant to the daylight as a last night’s
guttered candle,—all this may not seem a very seductive form of
temptation; but the majority of men in Basset found it fatally alluring when
encountered on their road toward four o’clock on a wintry afternoon; and
if any wife in Basset wished to indicate that her husband was not a
pleasure-seeking man, she could hardly do it more emphatically than by saying
that he didn’t spend a shilling at Dickison’s from one Whitsuntide
to another. Mrs Moss had said so of  her  husband more than once, when
her brother was in a mood to find fault with him, as he certainly was to-day.
And nothing could be less pacifying to Mr Tulliver than the behaviour of the
farmyard gate, which he no sooner attempted to push open with his riding-stick
than it acted as gates without the upper hinge are known to do, to the peril of
shins, whether equine or human. He was about to get down and lead his horse
through the damp dirt of the hollow farmyard, shadowed drearily by the large
half-timbered buildings, up to the long line of tumble-down dwelling-houses
standing on a raised causeway; but the timely appearance of a cowboy saved him
that frustration of a plan he had determined on,—namely, not to get down
from his horse during this visit. If a man means to be hard, let him keep in
his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and
with the command of a distant horizon. Mrs Moss heard the sound of the
horse’s feet, and, when her brother rode up, was already outside the
kitchen door, with a half-weary smile on her face, and a black-eyed baby in her
arms. Mrs Moss’s face bore a faded resemblance to her brother’s;
baby’s little fat hand, pressed against her cheek, seemed to show more
strikingly that the cheek was faded.
c8:p6.summary: The narrator exposes Mr Tulliver's false sense of security despite carrying a two-thousand-pound mortgage, his unconscious blindness to his sister's suffering, and his weakness in lending to Moss; the passage then provides a scathing sociological portrait of Basset parish, its poor soil, poverty, and the temptations of Dickison's public house.
c8:p6.best_quote: He had been always used to hear pleasant jokes about his advantages as a man who worked his own mill, and owned a pretty bit of land; and these jokes naturally kept up his sense that he was a man of considerable substance.

c25:p73.text:
Their mother came in now, and Maggie rushed away, that her burst of tears,
which she felt must come, might not happen till she was safe upstairs. They
were very bitter tears; everybody in the world seemed so hard and unkind to
Maggie; there was no indulgence, no fondness, such as she imagined when she
fashioned the world afresh in her own thoughts. In books there were people who
were always agreeable or tender, and delighted to do things that made one
happy, and who did not show their kindness by finding fault. The world outside
the books was not a happy one, Maggie felt; it seemed to be a world where
people behaved the best to those they did not pretend to love, and that did not
belong to them. And if life had no love in it, what else was there for Maggie?
Nothing but poverty and the companionship of her mother’s narrow griefs,
perhaps of her father’s heart-cutting childish dependence. There is no
hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants,
and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we
who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the
future lightened the blind sufferer’s present.
c25:p73.summary: Maggie rushes upstairs with bitter tears, feeling the world is hard and unkind; the narrator reveals her anguish: she expected love and tenderness from others as she imagines from books, but finds a harsh world where affection shows itself as fault-finding, and she sees no hope without love.
